newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican industry calls on army to fight crime.
newsitem.headline: Mexican industry calls on army to fight crime.

text.p: Mexican industrial leaders on Tuesday called for a greater role for the army in fighting crime.

"The correct thing to do is reduce delinquency and for that the participation of the army is needed," Jorge Marin Santillan, president of the Confederation of Industrial Chambers of Mexico (Concamin), told a news conference.
The concerns were raised at a Mexico City forum called Techno-Security 97.
Event organisers said more than 400 bands of organised crime operate in Mexico City, often preying on retailers and reselling stolen goods on the black market.
"The industry of organised crime, on top of robbing us, is an unfair competitor in selling our own products in the informal commercial sector," Marin said.

Some 30 percent of Mexican businesses suffered some type of theft in 1996 with losses in the millions of dollars, said Elena Maribona, director of the international exposition. Crime in Mexico was up 13 percent in 1996 over 1995, she said.
"The situation is alarming," Maribona said. "Organized crime has surpassed the capacity of the private and public police forces."
Violent crime has soared in Mexico since the economic recession caused by the sudden devaluation of the peso in December 1994, a convulsion that threw an estimated one million Mexican out of work.

Heavy security is a commonly accepted expense for Mexican businesses, most of whom hire armed security guards or invest in expensive alarm systems. But Maribona said about 43 percent of Mexico City businesses go without added security, leaving them particularly vulnerable.
